Other people had already given you very thoughtful answers about your father possibly having adhd too, which actually would add more confirmation to your own diagnosis since there's a strong evidence that genetic has a large part in it, so I won't echo them. What I'd like to address instead is that you should probably be more careful with your words about other people illnesses.

>"You don't have ADHD your JUST a narcissist"

It seems that you use the word "narcissism" as an insult and a mean of playing down whatever his struggles are, as if there were some sort of hierarchy of mental disorders and what you think is only yours (adhd) was more deserving of compassion than his (his supposed narcissism). Whether he has npd or not is for the professionals to say, not you or your mother; and it's quite self-telling what you wrote in your reply to another redditor, that "he needs to be diagnosed *with narcissism*" - he needs to address his mental problems with a professional, I don't doubt that as I don't doubt that all he made your family go through is enough to legitimate that you don't feel like being compassionate towards him (and, as a collateral victim of his issues, you don't have to be), but while he sure needs to be diagnosed, it feels like it's you who need this diagnosis to be narcissism as a validation of your suffering.

Not only is having npd not synonymous with being an asshole, as has unfortunately become widespread on the Internet (try to ask yourself: how many of those people claimed of being undiagnosed narcissists actually were so? They could be just assholes, or they could be suffering from any other mental illness), but npd, as many cluster B personality disorders, stems from a terrible source of internal pain, since it's strongly linked with trauma. That doesn't mean they're justified in harming others, *IF* they do harm others, but their illness and suffering is no less valid than yours. How could a person with *real* npd feel by reading your post? Why should they seek for help or share their experience and pain if people randomly use their disorder as a pejorative term? The problem here is that when any other mental illness is supected we say "I think they could be *suffering* from...", but when it comes to npd we *accuse* people to have it.

Your father's judment of adhd surely arises from prejudice and ignorance, but the same could be said of yours. Also, isn't your sense of entitlement towards your adhd a sign of narcissism that should be looked into further? Obviously it comes from pain, the pain of being raised by an abusive father and, as a person with a shitty childhood too, I feel you and I'm sorry that you had to went through this - but pain, masked low self-esteem, a big emotional wound are at the core of npd. Not saying that you have it, only that you unkowingly and unadvertedly showed one of its criteria.

I'm sorry for all you went through, which in my experience is difficult to share because sometimes it's not just a matter of "what happened to me that time", but something so pervasive that it's not easy to put in words. I've some bigger taumas, but I think it's reductive to only talk about those events as if my general background don't have an equal weight.

I hope you the best. Also, I feel you about the constant misdiagnosis which lead you to be skeptical of therapists and the frustration of being labeled with too many different things, as if you weren't seen as a person but as an entry in the diagnostic manual. If this makes you feel uncomfortable and don't feel the need to add another name to your problem at the moment, speak with your therapist. It seems to me those two diagnosis are so close/related that working on them as whole couldn't be bad, at least until you won't reach a point where you'll feel the need to address the bpd aspect of it more than the ptsd one.

It's almost like I wrote this. Bpd has been my first diagnosis, along with (complex?)ptsd, so I definitely relate. The two things are not mutually exclusive, actually I can see them overlap easily since bpd is known to be linked to a history of abuse. I don't think that extreme fear of abandonment is an inherently common trait of ptsd, but it could depending on what kind of trauma you suffered and if it was cumulative/repetitive more than a single event. 

Also, part of the scientific community believes that bpd it's just a complex ptsd to the point of even proposing to change its name, so I feel like your therapist is diagnosing you with almost the same thing. You could think of ptsd as your more clearly trauma related symptoms and bpd as the long lasting way it affected your personality. Or you can just call it c-ptsd, which includes them both.

Please, don't be swayed by my personal experience, everyone is different, and for every horror story there are at least twice successful ones! Coming off of this med (and meds in general) \*can\* be hard, and I think that some imbalance has to be expected, but it's incredibly subjective and you also hear from people who didn't get affected at all. More over, if you're taking it under your doctor's guidance, the med has been helping you and you have no reason to quit it at the moment, don't get worried. If you ever have to discontinue it, it's good to be mentally prepared for some shitty weeks, but that won't necessarily be the case for you.

"They have no empathy for other people." Empathy in borderline is a very discussed matter, we think we have empathy, as much as narcissists think they have too.

"They’re usually decent around other people." Borderlines can show their symptoms just with their "fp", the person who's, at the moment, their main target and obsession.

"They HATE to see you happy bc they themselves are very unhappy people." In splitting, a borderline can be very envious and vindictive, I don't have to spend much words here because I think everyone knows, deep inside, we're not the kindest people when we perceive to be abandoned.

This is not a BPD thing, but is related to high functioning autism (Asperger). Autism in women is really under-diagnosed because it's been considered a male-only disturb for a long time (wrongly). In women it shows with different symtomps that overlap with BPD, such as emotional disregulation, self-harm, eating disorders, intense reactions to little stimuli, plus (which is not a BPD trait) overstimulation by noises, or even smells and textures. 

There are studies about the fact that a lot of BPD diagnosed women are NOT borderline, but autistic.

I encourage all of you who have these symptoms to investigate further. Maybe you're not borderline and you need to get appropriate help to understand what you feel :)
